metadata.title: Apple is bringing a more 'mainstream' AI to its customers: Analyst

content.text:
00:00 Speaker A
Was this a great leap forward for Apple? Was it a catchup for Apple? How did you view it?
00:06 Speaker B
Yeah, I think there's there's two ways we see it. So obviously it's it's evolutionary. I'm not going to say that, you know, this is some giant leap and I think, you know, as we've talked about a number of times on these segments, we were never really in the camp that AI pulls any kind of super cycle, right, for devices. And I think most people now have aligned at that view that um obviously, you know, you buy hardware for certain reasons and you're probably not necessarily buying it for a whole host of AI-ish features that uh that come to your your your hardware.
00:26 Speaker B
So we think that this does two things. You know, we we know that the vast majority of consumers are still not doing what we'll just say like workflow automation, which is something we talk a lot about in enterprise, um in terms of stringing tasks together and a lot of the ROI that's going on in enterprise is from that productivity boost. The consumer side is very different, right? Most consumers have just been using something like Chat GBT, maybe Claude or Grock or what not for basic search. It's basically replaced Google for them.
00:51 Speaker B
And so I think there's still the opportunity to do these ease of use tasks, maybe boost efficiency, make things easier for you to do, string tasks on on the consumer side, but that's a very different set of things, right? around email, around maybe calendar, some of the things that Apple showed. So we think this is more about them bringing mainstream AI experiences to the consumer platform within their consumer apps and starting to give consumers some of that feel where AI disappears and just becomes more useful.
01:14 Speaker A
Yeah. I mean I mean what struck me as you were talking about that, as Dan was talking about some of the possibilities is like, this is stuff that I sort of expect the phone to do already. The next question becomes looking ahead, has this helped Apple future proof itself?
01:28 Speaker B
I think there's two parts. I think the main kind of takeaway is there's a threat to what we loosely call the the software control plane layer. So the thing in which you interface to interact with software and that's really what, you know, Open AI and Anthropic are trying to do with their, you know, chat surfaces is to become something that you interact with and it'll go connect to a whole slew of other software, right? And so there is something to that. Like not to say that you're still not going to use your smartphone, you're still not going to use your Mac or your PC, but the interface that you interact with, right? And so that's where the the question is, does the value accrue to something else, right? That sits that's a para platform to a platform you're using. And and that I would believe is is some kind of a risk.
02:07 Speaker B
I think what Apple did is actually very interesting here because you could argue and I think we're a bit of this of this position that it's actually going to be harder for the open AIs of the world and even anthropic to the degree that they would ever have consumer ambitions to be that interface that we're talking about in light of what Apple's just done. Because Apple will be the trusted source, the one who people will use. Siri becomes that control plane that I talked about, and thus Apple can maintain and preserve the value of their platforms with that kind of agent, you know, AI interaction versus others who might try to have usurped that from them.
